name: Ahijah
title: The Prophet from Shiloh
summary: The Shiloh prophet Ahijah was a central figure in the dramatic upheaval when the united Israelite kingdom was divided. It was through him that God announced His will to tear ten tribes away from David's house—conveyed through a striking symbolic act where Ahijah tore a new cloak into twelve pieces and gave ten of them to Jeroboam, son of Nebat. This prophetic gesture carried both a promise and an obligation: Jeroboam was offered a lasting dynasty, but only on the condition of obedience to the Lord's commands and covenant. The tragedy in Ahijah's prophetic ministry came to expression when he, now old and blind, was visited by Jeroboam's disguised wife. Her son Abijah lay deathly ill, yet Ahijah, guided by divine revelation, saw through the disguise and proclaimed a devastating judgment against Jeroboam's house. The king's widespread idolatry had rendered the conditional promise void. Ahijah's prophetic work was recorded in a separate writing, "the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite," which is referenced in Chronicles—a testimony to his high standing in Israel's prophetic tradition.

keyEvents.title: The Prophecy to Jeroboam about the Division of the Kingdom
keyEvents.description: Ahijah met Jeroboam on the road outside Jerusalem and performed a dramatic prophetic sign: he tore his new cloak into twelve pieces and gave ten of them to Jeroboam as a sign that God would give him rule over ten of the tribes of Israel. The biblical text notes that one tribe was to remain under the house of David, for the sake of Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Jeroboam's Wife Visits Ahijah
keyEvents.description: When Jeroboam's son Abijah fell ill, Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise to the now blind and elderly prophet Ahijah in Shiloh to inquire about the boy's fate. God had already revealed to Ahijah who the visitor was.

keyEvents.title: Judgment on the House of Jeroboam
keyEvents.description: Ahijah recognized Jeroboam's wife despite her disguise, having been revealed by God Himself, and proclaimed God's judgment against the house of Jeroboam. The judgment was crushing: all of Jeroboam's family would be wiped out because he had practiced idolatry, made other gods for himself, cast images, and thus led Israel into sin.

keyEvents.title: The Prophecy about Abijah's Death
keyEvents.description: Ahijah prophesied that Jeroboam's sick son Abijah would die the moment his mother's feet crossed the threshold at home. Abijah was to be the only one in Jeroboam's house to receive a dignified burial, because something good had been found in him toward the Lord.

keyEvents.title: Ahijah's Writings Mentioned in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Ahijah's prophecies and deeds were recorded in a writing known as 'the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite,' which is referenced as a historical source in Chronicles.

versions.summary: Ahijah (also known as Ahijah) was a prophet from Shiloh who lived around the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel. He is best known for prophesying that Jeroboam would become king over ten of the tribes of Israel, and later for pronouncing judgment on the house of Jeroboam because of idolatry.
versions.title: The Prophet from Shiloh
versions.reason: [minor] According to 1 Kgs 14:2 (LXX) and rabbinic tradition, Ahijah may be linked to the line of Ahitub, but the Hebrew text mentions no father. However, there is no biblical reference that explicitly names his father, so leaving it blank is acceptable. No change needed.; [minor] The description says "twelve pieces," which is correct according to 1 Kgs 11:30. However, it may be clarified that Jeroboam received ten pieces while the remaining two represented the tribes that remained under David's house (Judah and Benjamin).; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. Footnotes covering historical, linguistic, and theological aspects of Ahijah should be added.

versions.summary: Ahijah (also known as Ahija) was a prophet from Shiloh who served around the time of the division of Israel's kingdom. He is best known for his dramatic prophetic sign-act in which he tore a new robe into twelve pieces and gave Jeroboam ten of them, as a sign that God would give him dominion over ten of the tribes of Israel. Later, old and blind, Ahijah proclaimed God's judgment against the house of Jeroboam because of idolatry and apostasy. His prophecies and deeds were recorded in a separate book referred to in Chronicles.
versions.title: The Prophet from Shiloh
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is very similar to version 1 (the opening is identical). Since an earlier version exists, the text should be rephrased to avoid repetition and provide a fresher perspective.; [minor] The event "God's promise conditioned on obedience" strongly overlaps with the verses in the first event (verses 38–39 are already included in the first event). Consider merging it with the first event or clarifying the distinction.; [minor] Typo: 'teofourt' should be 'theophoric' (i.e., a name carrying a divine reference).; [minor] The meaning "brother of the Lord" is misleading. Ahijah (אֲחִיָּה) more precisely means "my brother is Yahweh" or "Yahweh is (my) brother." "Brother of the Lord" suggests something else and should be avoided or clarified.; [minor] The lifespan "around the 900s BC" is reasonable but could be specified further, e.g., "circa 960–900 BC," based on his ministry occurring both before and after the division of the kingdom (circa 930 BC).; [minor] The description states that "the remaining two pieces represented the tribes that would remain under David's house," but the text in 1 Kings 11:31–32 says Jeroboam received ten pieces and one piece was left (for Judah), not two. Some interpretations include Benjamin, but the biblical text explicitly mentions "one tribe." This should be nuanced.

versions.summary: Ahijah, also called Ahiah, was a prophet based in Shiloh who played a decisive role in the political and spiritual upheaval when the kingdom of Israel was divided. In a dramatic symbolic act, he tore a new robe into twelve pieces and gave Jeroboam ten of them—a powerful sign that God himself would tear most of the kingdom away from Solomon’s dynasty because of idolatry. Through Ahijah, God also conveyed a conditional promise to Jeroboam of a lasting dynasty if he remained faithful to the covenant. Later in life, old and blind, Ahijah was visited by Jeroboam’s disguised wife when their son Abijah lay sick. The prophet exposed her disguise and announced God’s crushing judgment against Jeroboam’s house, precisely because Jeroboam had failed in the obedience that was the condition for God’s blessing. Ahijah’s work was also recorded in a separate prophetic writing referred to in Chronicles, which testifies to his recognized standing among Israel’s prophets.

footnotes.text: The name Ahijah (Hebrew: אֲחִיָּה, Achiyyah) is a theophoric name meaning 'my brother is Yahweh' or 'Yahweh is (my) brother.' Such theophoric names were common in ancient Israel and testify to the bearer's connection with the God of Israel.

Shiloh (Hebrew: שִׁילֹה) was an important religious center in Israel where the tabernacle stood during the period of the judges and the early monarchy. The fact that Ahijah came from Shiloh links him to a long prophetic tradition associated with this place. Archaeological excavations at Khirbet Seilun have uncovered remains from several periods, including the Iron Age.

The symbolic action in which Ahijah tore his cloak into twelve pieces (1 Kings 11:29–31) is a typical example of a prophetic sign-act (Hebrew: אוֹת, ot) in the Old Testament. Such dramatic actions were used by the prophets to convey God's message in a visual and unforgettable way, as we also see with Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel.

The reference to 'the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite' in 2 Chronicles 9:29 suggests that written prophetic sources existed which the author of Chronicles had access to but which have not been preserved. This is one of several lost sources mentioned in the Old Testament and testifies to a richer literary tradition in ancient Israel than what has been handed down.

According to rabbinic tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 121b), Ahijah from Shiloh was very old and had lived since the time in Egypt. Some rabbinic sources claim that he was among those who left Egypt during the Exodus, which would make him extremely long-lived. This tradition underscores his authority as a prophet and his connection to a venerable spiritual heritage.

The relationship between ten and twelve tribes in Ahijah's prophecy raises an interesting calculation: Jeroboam received ten pieces, but the text mentions only 'one tribe' remaining for the house of David (1 Kings 11:32, 36). The missing twelfth tribe has been the subject of much discussion. Possible explanations include that Levi had no own territory, or that Benjamin was divided between the two kingdoms.
